statement: How many subsets $S$ of $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 20\}$, including the empty set, have the property that no number in $S$ is exactly twice another number in $S$?

choices.misconception: I handled the chains that start at 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 correctly but forgot the odd numbers 11 to 19, which are free to be in or out.
I thought at most one number could be taken from each doubling chain, so a chain of length k gave k + 1 choices.
I counted the allowed subsets of the chain 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 as 8 instead of 13.
I treated the 10 forbidden pairs (b, 2b) as independent, each ruling out a quarter of the subsets, so I got 2^20 times (3/4)^10, which is 3^10.

hints: Group the numbers so that doubling keeps you inside a group.

Every number is an odd number times a power of 2. The chain $m, 2m, 4m, \ldots$ for odd $m$ is a path in which only neighbours conflict, and different chains never interact. Count each chain separately and multiply.

The chains are $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$; $3, 6, 12$; $5, 10, 20$; $7, 14$; $9, 18$; and the singletons $11, 13, 15, 17, 19$. A chain of length $k$ has $a_k$ good subsets, where $a_1 = 2$, $a_2 = 3$ and $a_k = a_{k-1} + a_{k-2}$.

solutions.reliable: Write each number as $2^j m$ with $m$ odd. The condition only links $x$ and $2x$, which lie in the same chain $m, 2m, 4m, \ldots$, so the chains can be handled independently. In a chain of length $k$ we need a subset with no two neighbours. Let $a_k$ count these: either the last element is out ($a_{k-1}$ ways) or it is in and its neighbour is out ($a_{k-2}$ ways), with $a_1 = 2$, $a_2 = 3$. So $a_3 = 5$, $a_4 = 8$, $a_5 = 13$. The chains have lengths $5, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1$, giving $13 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 2^5 = 13 \cdot 25 \cdot 9 \cdot 32 = 93600$. Transferable idea: split a conflict structure into independent pieces, count each piece, and multiply.
